paras: The whitecap notice to Dennis Powell was a death threat posted at the gate of a Black landowner about two miles southwest of Brookhaven, Mississippi, in early December 1903. The typewritten notice ordered Powell to leave or suffer death, and the men who left it fired shots near his house; no one was reported hurt. The Brookhaven Leader reported it as a local item, and a Black correspondent at Brookhaven soon described a white-cap notice there, possibly the same one.

Powell owned a 40-acre place adjoining the Dunn place, bought from Chancery Clerk R. W. McNair. In the same days, citizens of neighboring Franklin County condemned midnight "shooting into houses and giving orders to the negroes" in their district and called a mass meeting at Meadville.

According to the Leader, Powell came into Brookhaven on the morning of December 2 and showed "a number of white friends" a notice he said he had found stuck on a stick in front of his gate. It read: "Negro you must leave this place at once or else suffer the penalty of death," and a coffin was drawn in lead pencil on the back. Powell said tracks showed only two men had posted it, and that they fired two or three shots near his house.
No report of arrests, an investigation or a later attack on Powell was found in either press.

The Leader ran the story on its front page as "Threatened With Death," relying on Powell's account and supposing that the posters lived nearby and were "playing 'white cap' for a special purpose," which it did not name.

The Baltimore Afro-American's December 12 column "Midnight's Musings," datelined Brookhaven, said its writer had looked at a notice served on "our people." It did not name the recipient but said he stayed home "prepared to fight," and it blamed "Red Necke" resentment of Black progress. Where the Leader offered no condemnation, the correspondent called for "an end put to this kind of lawlessness."

reader.title: Whitecap notice to Dennis Powell
bases: Two unidentified men posted a typed notice ordering Powell, a Black landowner, to leave on pain of death and fired shots near his house, which the local paper described as 'playing "white cap"' (A1).

No one was killed or injured; the notice threatened death, and Powell judged from tracks that only two men posted it (A1). No reason for the threat was stated beyond the paper's guess at an unnamed 'special purpose' (A1).

Only the Brookhaven Leader names Powell and describes the notice (A1); the Afro-American correspondent's account of a white-cap notice at Brookhaven (A4) fits but does not name the recipient, so it cannot be counted as independent confirmation.

accounts.label: Local paper, from Powell's report
accounts.gist: Powell found a typewritten death notice with a coffin drawing at his gate; two men posted it and fired shots near his house; the paper supposed local neighbors were 'playing "white cap" for a special purpose'.

accounts.label: Black correspondent
accounts.gist: A traveling correspondent at Brookhaven saw a white-cap notice served on a Black man who refused to leave and was armed to defend himself; the man is not named.

framing.detail: Short local item headed 'Threatened With Death', reporting Powell's account, noting his land purchase from a county official, and calling the act 'playing "white cap"' without condemnation.

The Afro-American's 'Midnight's Musings' set the notice in 'the country of white caps', blamed 'Red Necke' resentment of Black progress, and called for an end to the lawlessness while praising the recipient's armed resolve.

set_aside: White caps in southwestern Lincoln County shoot into the home of Eli Hilson and kill Henry Lisle; separate episodes.
Brookhaven wire, Dec. 21: Eli Hilson assassinated after disregarding a whitecap warning; 'second negro murdered by Whitecaps' in that part of Lincoln County within a month. Separate episode.
